headline: Highest risk is medium prompt-injection and data leakage via shared graph state; no direct evidence of a dangerous default interaction beyond orchestration wiring.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A is a stateful orchestration framework with write_filesystem, read_filesystem, broad network egress, and shared_state_with_other_instances via checkpointer; Agent B is a prompt-leak corpus that can supply attacker-controlled text. If A ingests B content into graph state or tools, prompt injection is plausible in default wiring. The interaction is inferred, not directly documented.
conditions: IF Agent A loads Agent B text into a node prompt or shared graph state
IF the orchestrator forwards B-produced text to a tool-using node without provenance checks
mitigations: Add a provenance tag to all B-derived text before graph ingestion
Insert a 1-step human review before any tool-using node consumes B content
Strip instructions from B text with a fixed allowlist parser
Disable shared checkpointer writes for untrusted inputs
requires-engineering: isolate untrusted content in a separate graph namespace

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A can read and write application-defined files and handle model provider API keys; Agent B is a prompt-leak source that may expose sensitive prompts if stored in the same workspace. Shared state or files could leak into outputs, but B has no network egress, so the main risk is workspace exposure rather than uncontrolled exfiltration. The pairwise pathway is inferred from A's storage surfaces.
conditions: IF Agent A persists B-derived prompts or secrets in application-defined files
IF those files are readable by any downstream node or operator
mitigations: Move B-derived artifacts to a separate directory with restrictive permissions
Redact secrets before writing graph state
Review file paths used by A for shared workspace overlap
Turn off persistence for sensitive runs
requires-engineering: add per-node data classification and access controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent A has write_filesystem and broad network egress; Agent B has no network egress, so they do not conflict on outbound network, but A's mutable filesystem and shared checkpointer can still collide with any files or state B consumes. Because B exposes no write surface, the conflict is narrower than high, yet overlapping mutable state remains plausible in default orchestration.
conditions: IF Agent B reads from files or state that Agent A also writes
IF multiple A instances share the same checkpointer namespace
mitigations: Assign separate working directories per agent
Namespace checkpointer keys by run ID
Avoid concurrent writes to shared artifacts
Use file locks around shared outputs
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency control to shared state

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent A can produce graph state and tool outputs that Agent B may treat as authoritative if wired together, and B's prompt-leak focus suggests it may render or reuse text without strong verification. No direct evidence shows B taking actions, so this is below high, but A-to-B propagation without a validation step is a realistic default orchestration failure.
conditions: IF Agent A's generated text is passed into Agent B as an instruction or summary
IF Agent B renders A output without an explicit verification step
mitigations: Insert a verification node between A and B
Require citations or structured schema from A before B consumes output
Mark A output as untrusted in the prompt template
Limit B to read-only summarization of A output
requires-engineering: add automated consistency checks between nodes

E_compliance.rationale: Agent A handles model provider API keys and application-defined graph state, while Agent B is source-available and unrunnable with no stated sensitive-data handling. No residency or certification mismatch is documented, so compliance risk is limited to generic logging/retention uncertainty rather than a concrete breach pathway.
conditions: IF the deployment stores regulated data in Agent A graph state
IF Agent B is later connected to the same regulated dataset
mitigations: Confirm whether regulated data enters the graph state
Keep secrets out of shared logs
Document retention for A's checkpointer
Do not connect B to regulated workloads without review
requires-engineering: add residency and retention policy enforcement
